title.en: Neurodiverse or neurodivergent? The words matter
title.ha: Neurodiverse ko neurodivergent? Kalmomin na da muhimmanci
title.yo: Neurodiverse tàbí neurodivergent? Àwọn ọ̀rọ̀ náà ṣe pàtàkì
title.ig: Neurodiverse ka neurodivergent? Okwu ndị a dị mkpa

summary.en: Two similar words with different meanings, and why we use both.
summary.ha: Kalmomi biyu masu kama da juna amma ma’anoninsu daban, da dalilin da ya sa muke amfani da su duka.
summary.yo: Ọ̀rọ̀ méjì tó jọra ṣùgbọ́n ìtumọ̀ wọn yàtọ̀, àti ìdí tí a fi ń lò méjèèjì.
summary.ig: Okwu abụọ yiri ibe ha mana nwere nkọwa dị iche, na ihe mere anyị ji eji ha abụọ.

posts.cover_alt: Abstract indigo illustration of connected ideas
posts.body:
Neurodiversity describes the natural variation in how human brains work. It is a fact about a group, like biodiversity. A classroom, a family or a country can be neurodiverse.

Neurodivergent describes an individual whose brain works differently from what is typically expected. That includes people who are autistic, have ADHD or dyslexia, and others. The term neurotypical describes people whose thinking fits that typical expectation.

The word neurodiversity was popularised in the late 1990s by the sociologist Judy Singer. The idea behind it is simple: differences in thinking are part of human variety, and people do better when environments adapt instead of expecting everyone to fit one mould.
posts.note: A person is neurodivergent. A community is neurodiverse.
posts.source: Singer, J. (1999). “Why can’t you be normal for once in your life?” In Disability Discourse. Open University Press.

title.en: Five signs a classroom isn’t working for a neurodivergent student
title.ha: Alamu biyar da ke nuna ajin karatu bai dace da ɗalibi mai bambancin kwakwalwa ba
title.yo: Àmì márùn-ún tí kíláàsì kò bá akẹ́kọ̀ọ́ tí ọpọlọ rẹ̀ yàtọ̀ mu
title.ig: Ihe ịrịba ama ise na-egosi na klaasị adịghị arụ ọrụ maka nwa akwụkwọ ụbụrụ ya dị iche

summary.en: Often it is not about effort. It is about the environment.
summary.ha: Sau da yawa ba game da ƙoƙari ba ne. Yanayi ne.
summary.yo: Ó pọ̀ ìgbà, kì í ṣe nípa ìsapá. Àyíká ni.
summary.ig: Ọtụtụ oge, ọ bụghị banyere mgbalị. Gburugburu ya bụ.

posts.cover_alt: Abstract green illustration of a calm learning space
posts.body:
A student who looks distracted, restless or withdrawn may be reacting to noise, unclear instructions or long stretches of passive listening. Labelling them lazy hides the real cause.

Watch for repeated incomplete work despite clear ability, strong distress at changes in routine, avoiding reading or writing aloud, difficulty following spoken multi-step instructions, and exhaustion after school.

Many helpful changes cost nothing: written and spoken instructions together, a quiet corner, extra time, and breaking tasks into steps. The Universal Design for Learning framework recommends offering more than one way to take in information and show understanding.
posts.note: Change the task or space first, then judge the student.
posts.source: CAST (2018). Universal Design for Learning Guidelines version 2.2. udlguidelines.cast.org

title.en: How to support a neurodivergent colleague
title.ha: Yadda za a tallafa wa abokin aiki mai bambancin kwakwalwa
title.yo: Bí a ṣe lè ṣe àtìlẹ́yìn fún alábàáṣiṣẹ́ tí ọpọlọ rẹ̀ yàtọ̀
title.ig: Otu esi akwado onye ọrụ ibe ụbụrụ ya dị iche

summary.en: Small, specific adjustments, agreed with the person, go a long way.
summary.ha: Ƙananan gyare-gyare na musamman, da aka amince da mutumin, na taimakawa sosai.
summary.yo: Àwọn àtúnṣe kékeré tó ṣe pàtó, tí a gbà pẹ̀lú ẹni náà, ń ṣe ànfàní púpọ̀.
summary.ig: Mgbanwe nta doro anya, nke e kwekọrịtara na onye ahụ, na-enye aka nke ukwuu.

posts.cover_alt: Abstract gold illustration of a connected workplace
posts.body:
Do not guess what someone needs. Ask: what helps you do your best work? Needs differ widely, even between two people with the same diagnosis.

Common adjustments include written follow-ups after meetings, agendas shared in advance, flexible hours, quieter workspaces and clear, direct feedback.

Research on neurodiversity at work argues that many neurodivergent people bring strengths such as sustained focus, pattern recognition and creative problem solving, but that these show up only when the workplace fits them. Treat strengths and support needs as both true.
posts.note: Ask, agree, write it down, and review it together.
posts.source: Doyle, N. (2020). Neurodiversity at work: a biopsychosocial model and the impact on working adults. British Medical Bulletin, 135(1), 108–125.

title.en: If you think your child may be neurodivergent, where to start
title.ha: Idan kana tsammanin yaronka yana da bambancin kwakwalwa, ga inda za ka fara
title.yo: Tí o bá rò pé ọmọ rẹ lè ní ọpọlọ tó yàtọ̀, níbi tí o ti lè bẹ̀rẹ̀
title.ig: Ọ bụrụ na ị chere na nwa gị nwere ụbụrụ dị iche, ebe ị ga-esi malite

summary.en: A calm first-steps guide for parents and carers.
summary.ha: Jagorar matakan farko cikin natsuwa ga iyaye da masu kulawa.
summary.yo: Ìtọ́sọ́nà ìgbésẹ̀ àkọ́kọ́ ní ìdákẹ́jẹ́ẹ́ fún òbí àti olùtọ́jú.
summary.ig: Ntụziaka usoro mbụ n’udo maka nne na nna na ndị na-elekọta.

posts.cover_alt: Abstract rose illustration of a supportive first step
posts.body:
Write down what you notice at home and at school: when it happens, how often and what helps. Specific examples are more useful to a professional than general worries.

Speak to your child’s teacher and then to a qualified professional, such as a paediatrician, child psychiatrist or clinical psychologist. Diagnosis should come from a trained clinician, not from online checklists.

The World Health Organization’s ICD-11 describes autism spectrum disorder and ADHD under neurodevelopmental conditions, and clinicians use criteria like these when assessing. While you wait, you can already adjust routines, reduce sensory overload and keep communication kind and clear.
posts.note: You do not need a diagnosis to start helping.
posts.source: World Health Organization (2019). ICD-11, Chapter 6: Neurodevelopmental disorders. icd.who.int
